title: Logic and Proof Strategies
summary: This unit covers predicate logic (Prädikatlogik), logical connectives (Junktoren), quantifiers (Quantoren), and valid inferences (gültige Schlussfolgerungen). You will learn to evaluate conditionals (Konditionale) and if-then-else constructs (If-Then-Else-Verknüpfungen), distinguish sufficient and necessary conditions (hinreichende und notwendige Bedingungen), and analyze syllogisms (Syllogismen) and countermodels (Gegenmodelle). Finally, you will practice systems of linear equations (lineare Gleichungssysteme) and key proof strategies (Beweisstrategien), such as direct proof (direkter Beweis), contraposition (Kontraposition), and proof by contradiction (Widerspruch).
concepts: Domain and variable binding (Grundmenge und Variablenbindung)
Logical connectives and truth tables (Junktoren und Wahrheitstabellen)
Venn and Euler diagrams (Venn- und Euler-Diagramme)
keyFacts: Predicate logic describes properties of objects and relations between them, using variables and quantifiers.
To evaluate a predicate, the domain, the meanings of the predicates, and the assignments to free variables must be specified.
A conditional is false only for the assignment $A=w$ and $B=f$; when $A$ is false, it is true regardless of $B$.
“Or” is inclusive, whereas “either A or B” is exclusive.
If-Then-Else is equivalent to $(A∧B)∨(¬A∧C)$ and to $(A⇒B)∧(¬A⇒C)$.
A propositional formula is a tautology if it is true under every assignment.
For $A⇒B$, $A$ is sufficient for $B$ and $B$ is necessary for $A$. In set-theoretic terms, the truth set of $A$ is contained entirely in the truth set of $B$.
The four basic forms of restricted quantifiers are: all, not all, some, and none.
A universal statement does not automatically assert that there is any object in the restricted domain.
A witness confirms an existence claim; a counterexample refutes a universal statement.
The negations of the quantifiers satisfy $¬∀xP(x)≡∃x¬P(x)$ and $¬∃xP(x)≡∀x¬P(x)$.
A Venn diagram shows all combinations of membership and nonmembership; an Euler diagram represents specific set relations through the placement of its curves.
A syllogism is valid if, whenever its premises are true, its conclusion cannot be false.
From $3x+4y=0$ and $-2x+3y=17$, it follows that $y=3$ and $x=-4$.
Modus ponens, modus tollens, and chaining conditionals are valid quantifier-free rules of inference.
Direct proof, contraposition, contradiction, and proof of equivalence are important proof strategies; induction is mentioned only as a strategy.

questions.prompt: What does predicate logic describe?

options.text: Only truth tables for two statements that have already been fully assigned truth values
Properties of objects and relations between them, using variables and quantifiers
Only the order of instructions in programs
Only number sets, without statement forms

questions.explanation: Predicate logic extends propositional logic with variables and quantifiers to describe properties and relations.

questions.prompt: A predicate is a ___ statement form.
questions.explanation: A predicate contains parameters, such as “$x$ is an integer,” and receives a truth value only after an object is substituted.

questions.prompt: Which assumptions are important when evaluating a predicate? More than one answer may be correct.

options.text: Free variables are assigned values or bound by quantifiers.
Every predicate must be true for every object.
There must always be a truth table with exactly two variables.
The meanings of the predicates being used are specified.

questions.explanation: The domain, the meanings of the predicates, and the binding or assignment of free variables determine the evaluation. Universal truth and a truth table with two variables are not required.

questions.prompt: “Or” is inclusive, whereas “either A or B” is exclusive.
questions.explanation: Inclusive or is true even when both statements are true. Exclusive or is false when both statements are true.

questions.prompt: For which assignment is the conditional $A\Rightarrow B$ false?
questions.explanation: A conditional is false exactly when the antecedent is true and the consequent is false.

questions.prompt: Which phrasing describes a biconditional?
questions.explanation: A biconditional is phrased as “$A$ if and only if $B$” and includes both directions.

questions.prompt: “If $A$, then $B$, otherwise $C$” selects the truth value of $B$ or $C$ depending on ___.
questions.explanation: If $A$ is true, $B$ is used; if $A$ is false, $C$ is used.

questions.prompt: Which statements distinguish the logical operation from a program branch? More than one answer may be correct.

options.text: The logical operation compares truth values.
The logical operation always executes both program branches.
In a program, a condition $A$ typically appears before the branch.

questions.explanation: Logical operations compute truth values. Programs, by contrast, execute one branch of instructions depending on the condition.

questions.prompt: Which formula describes “All objects with $R$ also have $P$”?
questions.explanation: For every object: if it satisfies the restriction $R$, then it also has the property $P$.

source.heading: Alle Objekte mit R haben auch P

questions.prompt: What does “Some $R$ are $P$” mean in this course?

options.text: At least one object is both $R$ and $P$.
More than half of the objects are both $R$ and $P$.
Some, but not all, objects are both $R$ and $P$.

questions.explanation: Here, “some” means at least one object, not necessarily more than one and not “some but not all.”

questions.prompt: In quantifier diagrams, overlapping circles show the possible regions of membership. Gray regions are empty or excluded; white regions may or may not be empty. A dot marks an object whose existence is asserted. Gray means that the marked region is ___.
questions.explanation: Gray marks a region in which no object may lie. A dot, by contrast, represents an asserted witness.

questions.prompt: For truth values $A,B,C\in\{w,f\}$, let $I(A,B,C)$ be defined as follows: If $A$ is true, then $I(A,B,C)=B$; if $A$ is false, then $I(A,B,C)=C$. Compute $I(A,B,C)$ for $A=f$, $B=w$, and $C=f$.

options.text: $A$ and $C$ are both false, so the result is always $w$

questions.explanation: Since $A=f$, the else branch is selected. It returns $C=f$.

questions.prompt: Which formula describes exactly the cases where “If $A$, then $B$, otherwise $C$” is true?
questions.explanation: If $A$ is true, $B$ must hold; if $A$ is false, $C$ must hold. This gives $(A\land B)\lor(\neg A\land C)$.

questions.prompt:
What does this code print?

```python
A = True

if A:
    print("Anweisung b wird ausgeführt")
else:
    print("Anweisung c wird ausgeführt")
```
questions.explanation: $A$ is true, so only the first branch of instructions is executed.

questions.prompt: For $x=1$, the statement $x\in\mathbb{Z}\Rightarrow x/2\in\mathbb{Z}$ is ___.
questions.explanation: $1\in\mathbb{Z}$ is true, but $1/2\notin\mathbb{Z}$. This is exactly the false case of a conditional.

questions.prompt: Which condition is sufficient for $x\in\mathbb{Z}$?
questions.explanation: From $x/2\in\mathbb{Z}$ it follows that $x=2\cdot(x/2)\in\mathbb{Z}$. Integer-valued $x$ alone, however, does not guarantee that $x/2$ is an integer.

questions.prompt: Which formula formalizes “Some positive real numbers have square 4”?
questions.explanation: “Some” requires an existential quantifier. The witness must be both positive and have square 4.

questions.prompt: Which assessment is correct? $\forall x\in\mathbb{Q}:x^2\ne2$ and $\forall x\in\mathbb{R}:x^2\ne2$.

options.text: The first is false and the second is true.
The first is true and the second is false.

questions.explanation: The inequality holds for rational $x$, while $x=\sqrt{2}$ is a real counterexample to the second universal statement.

questions.prompt: How is “Not all $R$ are $P$” formalized?
questions.explanation: “Not all” means that at least one $R$ exists that is not $P$. This witness is a counterexample to the universal statement.

questions.prompt: Which objects play the respective roles of proof or refutation in these examples? More than one answer may be correct.

options.text: $d=1$ is a counterexample to “All integers are even.”
$x=2$ is a witness for “Some positive real numbers have square 4.”
The unsuccessful attempt $x=1$ refutes the existence of a positive real $x$ with square 4.

questions.explanation: $1$ is an integer but not even, and $2$ is positive real with square 4. $\sqrt{2}$ is not a rational witness, and one unsuccessful attempt does not refute an existence claim.

questions.prompt: What solution results for the system of equations $3x+4y=0$ and $-2x+3y=17$?
questions.explanation: Adding the scaled equations gives $17y=51$, so $y=3$. Substituting into $3x+4y=0$ gives $x=-4$.

questions.prompt: Which conclusion follows validly from “Some pigs can fly” and “All pigs are animals”?
questions.explanation: A flying pig is also an animal, and thus remains a witness for “Some animals can fly.” Nothing follows about Miss Piggy or about all animals.

questions.prompt: Which statements about $x\in\mathbb{Z}$ and $x/2\in\mathbb{Z}$ are correct? More than one answer may be correct.
questions.explanation: If $x/2$ is an integer, then $x$ is an integer, so this condition is sufficient. Conversely, $x$ must be an integer if $x/2$ is an integer; integer-valued $x$ alone is not enough.

questions.prompt: Every conditional $A\Rightarrow B$ is a tautology.
questions.explanation: A conditional is a tautology only if it is true under every assignment. The assignment $A=w$, $B=f$ makes every such conditional false.

questions.prompt: Which condition describes exactly the cases where “If $A$, then $B$, otherwise $C$” is true?

options.text: $B$ and $C$ are both true, independently of $A$.
$A$ and $C$ are true, or $A$ is false and $B$ is true.
At least one of the statements $A$, $B$, and $C$ is true.
$A$ and $B$ are true, or $A$ is false and $C$ is true.

questions.explanation: Within $A$, only $B$ matters; outside $A$, only $C$ matters. Therefore, exactly $A\land B$ and $\neg A\land C$ are true.

questions.prompt: Use the following definitions for this question: A Venn diagram shows all combinations of membership and nonmembership in the sets under consideration as regions. An Euler diagram represents specific set relations through the placement of its curves; not all combinations need to appear as regions. In the quantifier diagrams, the circles remain overlapping, and excluded regions are marked in gray. Which statements are correct? More than one answer may be correct.

options.text: In an Euler diagram, all combinations must appear as distinct regions.
In quantifier diagrams, excluded regions are marked in gray while the circles remain overlapping.
A Venn diagram shows all combinations of membership and nonmembership in the sets under consideration.
An Euler diagram represents specific set relations through the placement of its curves.

questions.explanation: Venn diagrams show all combinations of membership. Euler diagrams show specific set relations; quantifier diagrams mark excluded regions in gray and keep the circles overlapping.

questions.prompt: Which is a counterexample to “Every real number whose square is 9 is positive”?
questions.explanation: $(-3)^2=9$, but $-3$ is not positive. Thus, $-3$ refutes the universal statement.

questions.prompt: From $x^2=2$, for real $x$, it follows that both the positive and the ___ root must be considered.
questions.explanation: The real solutions of $x^2=2$ are $x=\sqrt{2}$ and $x=-\sqrt{2}$. Naming only the positive root would be incomplete.

questions.prompt: Which quantifier transformations are logically equivalent? More than one answer may be correct.
questions.explanation: The first three formulas are the stated negation rules for quantifiers. The last formula confuses existence with the absence of counterexamples.

questions.prompt: When is an argument logically valid?

options.text: When the premises are true in reality.
When, given true premises, the conclusion cannot be false.
When at least one premise is false.
When the conclusion sounds especially plausible.

questions.explanation: Validity describes the form of an argument: there must be no case with true premises and a false conclusion. The actual truth of individual premises is irrelevant to this.

questions.prompt: An argument can be invalid even though its conclusion is true in a particular situation.
questions.explanation: Invalid means only that the conclusion does not necessarily follow from the premises. It may still happen to be true.

source.heading: Vier eigene Beispiele: Kinder, Benehmen und Geschenke

questions.prompt: What lower bound for $-x^3+4x+1$ follows from $0\le x\le2$ in a direct proof?
questions.explanation: We have $x(2-x)(2+x)\ge0$, so $-x^3+4x+1=x(2-x)(2+x)+1\ge1$. In particular, the required positivity follows.

questions.prompt: Which statement is the contrapositive of $A\Rightarrow B$?
questions.explanation: The contrapositive negates both statements and reverses their direction: $A\Rightarrow B$ is equivalent to $\neg B\Rightarrow\neg A$.

questions.prompt: Which formula is logically equivalent to $A\Rightarrow B$?
questions.explanation: The conditional can be written as $\neg A\lor B$. The form $A\lor\neg B$ reverses the roles of antecedent and consequent.

questions.prompt: Which statements about biconditionals and exclusive or are correct? More than one answer may be correct.

options.text: $A\oplus B$ is true exactly when $A$ and $B$ have the same truth value.
The conditional is symmetric in $A$ and $B$.

questions.explanation: A biconditional consists of both directions of implication. Exclusive or is true exactly when the truth values differ; a conditional is asymmetric.

questions.prompt: The sets $\mathbb{N}$, $\mathbb{Z}$, and $\mathbb{Q}$ are countable, while $\mathbb{R}$ is uncountable.
questions.explanation: This classification of number sets is among the fundamental statements about countability.

questions.prompt: Given $\forall x\,(R(x)\Rightarrow P(x))$ and $\exists x\,(R(x)\land Q(x))$, which conclusion necessarily follows?
questions.explanation: The witness for $R\land Q$ also satisfies $P$ by the universal statement. The same witness therefore establishes $\exists x\,(P\land Q)$.

questions.prompt:
For $A,B,C\in\{w,f\}$, let $
eg X$ denote the negation of $X$; $X\land Y$ is $w$ exactly when both values are $w$. The conditional $X\Rightarrow Y$ is $f$ exactly when $X=w$ and $Y=f$. Define $I(A,B,C)$ as $B$ if $A=w$, and $C$ otherwise; $K(A,B)$ as $B$ if $A=w$, and $w$ otherwise; and $E(A,B)$ as $B$ if $A=w$, and $
eg B$ otherwise. Also let $V(A,B,C)=(A\Rightarrow B)\land(
eg A\Rightarrow C)$. For $A=f$, $B=f$, and $C=w$: Which of the following four statements are true? Check each statement individually and select all that are true.
questions.explanation: Since $A=f$, we have $I(A,B,C)=C=w$, $K(A,B)=w$, and $E(A,B)=\neg B=w$. For $V$, we have $A\Rightarrow B=w$ and $\neg A\Rightarrow C=w\Rightarrow w=w$, so $V=w$. Therefore, exactly a and c are true.

questions.prompt:
Which situation is a countermodel to this argument?

“Some pigs can fly. Miss Piggy is a pig. Therefore, Miss Piggy can fly.”

options.text: All pigs fly, but Miss Piggy is not a pig
Miss Piggy flies and every pig is an animal
A flying pig $d$ and a non-flying Miss Piggy
Only a non-flying Miss Piggy, but no flying pig

questions.explanation: The premises remain true if another pig $d$ flies and Miss Piggy does not fly. This makes the conclusion false, so the argument is invalid.

questions.prompt: In the calculation for the statement “$3n+2$ is odd $\Rightarrow n$ is odd,” $n=2k$ is substituted. What does this prove?

options.text: The contrapositive: If $n$ is even, then $3n+2$ is even.
A biconditional between being even and being odd.
The converse: If $3n+2$ is even, then $n$ is even.
The original statement itself, without using a negation.

questions.explanation: From $n=2k$ it follows that $3n+2=2(3k+1)$, so the expression is even. This is exactly the contrapositive of the original claim.

questions.prompt: Which rules of inference are valid? More than one answer may be correct.

options.text: From $A\Rightarrow B$ and $\neg A$, infer $\neg B$.
From $A\Rightarrow B$ and $\neg B$, infer $\neg A$.

questions.explanation: a is modus ponens and b is modus tollens. The last two forms are invalid converses or misapplications of the conditional.

questions.prompt: Which proof strategy fits the following approach: assume $0\le x\le2$ and derive $-x^3+4x+1>0$ directly?
questions.explanation: In a direct proof, the hypothesis is assumed and the claim is derived through algebraic transformations and inferences.

questions.prompt: To prove $A\Leftrightarrow B$ in both directions, show $A\Rightarrow B$ and ___.
questions.explanation: A biconditional is exactly the conjunction of the two directions of implication.

questions.prompt: The domain consists of children. Lea is a child. Every child who behaves well gets a gift. Lea gets a gift. Which additional rule guarantees that you can conclude that Lea behaves well?

options.text: All children who behave well get a gift.
All children who get a gift behave well.

questions.explanation: The additional rule implies that, for every child, anyone who gets a gift behaves well. Since Lea is a child and gets a gift, it follows that Lea behaves well.

questions.prompt: Your navigation system checks: “If the road is closed, then I take a detour.” Which logical statement does this express?
questions.explanation: The rule has the form “If $A$, then $B$,” so it is a conditional. It does not automatically assert that a detour may be taken only when a road is closed.

questions.prompt: A database needs to find all customers who are adults and have a premium plan. Which logical connective fits the filter condition?

options.text: A restricted quantifier over all records found
“Adult or premium” in the inclusive sense: $A\lor B$

questions.explanation: Both conditions must be satisfied at the same time, so the filter uses logical AND. A conditional would not express the same selection condition.

questions.prompt: How many rows does a complete truth table for five propositional variables need?
questions.explanation: Each variable has two possible truth values. Therefore, there are $2^5=32$ assignments and thus 32 rows.

questions.prompt: Is this correct: A messaging app can use a universal statement to say that all messages with a particular property are checked, without thereby asserting that any such message exists.
questions.explanation: A universal statement such as “All $R$ are $P$” does not, by itself, guarantee that there is any object with $R$. Existence would have to be asserted separately.

questions.prompt: In Sudoku, you check that a number does not appear more than once in a row, column, or box. Which concept helps most directly?

options.text: A restricted universal statement about the relevant cells or pairs of cells

questions.explanation: The condition can be formulated as a statement about all relevant cells or pairs of cells: distinct cells must not contain the same number. A single duplicate is a counterexample.

questions.prompt: How many different 4-digit PINs are possible if each position can be any digit from 0 to 9 and leading zeros are allowed?
questions.explanation: Each of the four positions has 10 possible digits. The four positions are variables over the same finite domain, so there are $10^4=10\,000$ combinations.

questions.prompt: A static rule checker claims: “For every variable used, it has been declared beforehand.” It finds a variable that is used but not declared. What have you found?

options.text: A witness confirming the universal statement
A necessary condition that is automatically satisfied
A counterexample to the claimed universal statement

questions.explanation: The rule makes a claim about every variable used. A single variable that is used but not declared is enough to refute the universal statement.

questions.prompt: How many different bit patterns does a field of 12 bits have if each bit can be 0 or 1?
questions.explanation: Each of the 12 bits has two possible values. Therefore, there are $2^{12}=4096$ different assignments, or bit patterns.

questions.prompt: An online shop uses the rules: “If payment is authorized, the order is released. If the order is released, a confirmation appears.” Which rule of inference yields “If payment is authorized, a confirmation appears”?
questions.explanation: From $A\Rightarrow B$ and $B\Rightarrow C$, it follows that $A\Rightarrow C$. This is chaining conditionals. For a confirmation to actually appear, payment must also be authorized.

questions.prompt: Is this correct: If a check-digit rule claims that every number in a particular set satisfies the rule, one specific rejected number is enough to serve as a counterexample to that universal statement.
questions.explanation: A single specific number that fails the rule refutes the general claim that every number in the set under consideration satisfies the rule.
